tiles.title: Things to know about the the unit and CLUE

text:
Welcome to the Neural Engineering unit!

Before you get started with this lesson, we wanted to give you some general information about CLUE and the unit.

CLUE user guide: there is a lot to know about CLUE. We are working on simplifying a user guide, which you can find here. If there is anything you want to know that you can't find there, please reach out to our team and will will explain it and add it into the guide.

Resources for each lesson, like slides and handouts, can be found here. (We will link to specific folders or files as needed the teacher guide).

Please feel welcome to download them and make changes. We have added suggestions for where you may want to make changes as well.

If you make suggestions, we would really appreciate it if you sent them to us!

When you access the lessons as a teacher, you will find a solutions tab. This lesson doesn't exactly have "solutions," but toggling the solutions button on will give you additional tips and information about the lessons, such as where to have class discussions, possible ideas that students might have, and other tips and suggestions.

objects.text: Solutions tab gives additional info about lessons, that will show up in green throughout the lesson

text:
This unit combines life sciences, engineering, and computational thinking! You can see a unit overview here.

It is designed to take 17 classes (55 minutes long). However, there are opportunities for modification: it can be both longer and shorter, as needed. We will give more information in each lesson, but here are some big picture ideas:

  • Extensions: You may want to include benchmark lessons about key life sciences concepts in this unit if you want to embed it within an existing unit about the muscular or nervous systems. If you are in an engineering class, you may want to give students additional time to make more complex prototypes (e.g., 3D printing)
  • Reductions: Some lessons may be too simple for more advanced life sciences classes and can be cut. Additionally, lessons are grouped in "prototypes" and are designed so that each prototype is a convenient end point if you are short on time (although we recommend you add L4.4 even if you need to end the unit early).

The unit is designed around prototypes, to emphasize the authentic nature of engineering: students will be making more and more complex prototypes at each stage!

The emphasis is on engaging with engineering design. Specifically, we want to highlight to students that there are lots of ways to solve problems. The the students will build their own grippers, and they will be supported to develop a variety of different codes.

There will be lots of opportunities for collaboration, as well as for class discussion. We know that you may not yet feel totally comfortable with Dataflow, the coding language, and so we are adding images, examples, and explanations in the "solutions" tab and in the materials for each unit (e.g., the slides) that will help you navigate the students' questions.

This is a collaborative unit. We have set up the unit such that some work will be done in pairs, and some will be done in small groups (ideally two pairs, although depending on your class size/dynamics you can adjust the group size).

When students log in, they are prompted to join a group. They should make sure that they are in the same group with just their group-mates (typically two pairs). If they choose the wrong group, they can change groups by clicking on the group button on the top right.

  • In the "teacher view" you can also see all the groups and move students from group to group.
  • The groups are important because a new feature in CLUE is "group documents" --> students will be able to work together at certain points in the unit.

In Lesson 1.1, students are introduced to the unit through learning about what their hand does and developing their initial prototype.

They do not yet work with Dataflow or with hardware (spiker:bit or servo) or collect their own data - their initial prototype is fully mechanical.

Lesson 1.1 is expected to take two class periods. (More information in the "instructional sequence" tab)

Handouts and modifications:

  • Characters: There are currently six possible "characters." They each have different needs (e.g., there is variation in the limb differences that they have, as well as their needs). However, these are in a handout that can be modified so if you want to give your students fewer characters (or add additional ones) you can make modifications there.
  • Mechanical prototypes: Our team tested a lot of prototypes, and we now have instructions for several different options (we will bring the necessary materials). These are also in a handout - if you would like to provide fewer options to your students, you can remove the ones you do not want to offer from the handout.
  • We also have handouts for the instructions, which also include materials lists (we will bring materials!). Once each group decides which prototype they want to work on, you can give them the relevant instructions sheet. They instructions are designed as a guide: teams should modify them, and we have provided suggestions in the instructions for modifications (e.g., a different number of "fingers" or joints.
